item.title: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
item.description: YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google . At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike button being absent for them. Right now, for me, the dislike button sits right next to the like button under a video. item.title: Judge dismisses Sam Altman’s sister’s sexual abuse lawsuit
item.description: On Tuesday, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the lawsuit Ann Altman filed last year alleging that her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, had sexually abused her throughout her childhood. As reported earlier by The Guardian , the judge wrote that over the past year, Ann had failed to appear for an independent medical examination or meet other deadlines despite warnings that it would result in the case being dismissed. When the case was filed last year, a statement shared by Sam Altman, his mother, and his brothers said, "Annie has made deeply hurtful and entirely untrue claims about our family, and especially Sam… All of these claim … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Indian certification authority eMudhra’s private keys compromised – one of them was the number ‘4’
item.description: Tragically simple private keys used by a certification authority based in India have been compromised, meaning the 60-million-plus certs it has issued can’t be trusted and necessitating a massive clean-up job. The CA of concern in this case is called eMudhra, which boasts of having issued over 60 million digital certificates to help usher in a world of digital trust. The company has instead panicked the world. News of the company’s errors appeared on Tuesday in a post by Dennis Jackson, a member of Mozilla’s cryptography engineering team. “On Saturday, October 17, at 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report from a community member that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had been compromised,” he wrote . “These keys could allow attackers to issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites they do not control.” Or as Cloudflare put it , “an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic.” Jackson has since elaborated on the incident and the response, which has thankfully seen Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple remediate the issue so their browsers won’t rely on the certificates – at least after users install an update. He also reports that eMudhra has revoked the certs, and lists many FOSS projects that have issued updates that mean they won’t recognize certs from eMudhra. That’s welcome, but sadly certs signed with these private keys are still out there and many services rely on them. Browser makers are set up to detect and reject bad certs. Others who relied on them may not be, and will likely need to dig into their environments to see if they rely on certs signed by eMudhra. Developer Geoffrey Huntley has offered some advice on automating that process. At the time of writing, eMudhra has not responded to The Register ’s inquiries about the incident and its security practices. The latter question is of great interest because security researcher Scott Helme analyzed eMudhra’s certs and found one the private keys it used “is the number 4.” “Not a number that starts with 4, or the number 4 followed by a few hundred random digits, just, 4... Another one is 56, and another is 115. I know, because I recovered all of them from their public certificates on my laptop just now, and it took less than a second,” Helme wrote. Other researchers have found private keys including the numbers 66, 155, 156, 230 and 237. Those are vastly inadequate keys, because they’re easy to guess, making all certs issued by eMudhra susceptible to brute force attacks. As Helme put it: “A P-384 private key should be a random 384-bit number, which gives you 2³⁸⁴ possibilities (or roughly 10¹¹⁵), so nobody is ever going to search that.” This is a developing story and The Register will update it as more information becomes available. ®

item.description: Influencer Nick Shirley listens as US President Donald Trump makes an announcement on fraud in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 20, 2026. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday that the Trump administration was giving right-wing YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million bounty program for members of the public to report fraud. Shirley lingered in parking lots and asked to enter childcare centers, taking refusals as evidence that the centers weren't actually caring for children. item.title: Merging SpaceX and Tesla would be a "good idea," Musk says
item.description: Elon Musk said Tuesday that he would like to see the consolidation of his business empire by formally merging his two largest companies, SpaceX and Tesla. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said of a potential merger. He was speaking during a question-and-answer period as part of SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call. Musk said, ultimately, it not his decision. "But at the end of the day the shareholders have to be supportive of this." Musk's talk of a merger comes after a busy year in which SpaceX already acquired Musk's artificial intelligence firm, xAI, in February. In June, SpaceX went public with the largest initial public offering on record. Read full article Comments

item.title: Auto tech startup claims it traced hack attempt back to rival's IP address
item.description: An automotive tech startup claims that its IT systems were attacked by individuals trying to steal its driving model, and that those attacks came from an IP address associated with a rival in the space. The tech startup, IQ.Lvbs, described the alleged security incident in a recent blog post . On October 3, IQ.Lvbs introduced the private beta of NovaSpark , the first model for the company's IQ.Pilot app, in the Comma.ai Discord channel. They put it in that channel because the model requires the use of Comma.ai's camera hardware, which is built for self-driving vehicles. From there, things got weird. "From October 7 to 14, we faced repeated attempts to steal NovaSpark, access users’ devices and private driving files, and exploit our sign-in system," the IQ.Lvbs blog post claims. "The first requests came from an IP assigned to Comma.ai Inc." In addition, on October 8 – shortly after the alleged attacks began – somebody banned IQ.Lvbs' team from the Comma.ai Discord channel. Posts on the IQ.Pilot Discord channel indicate that individuals doing private beta testing for IQ.Lvbs have also been banned from that channel. One of the three people involved in IQ.Lvbs, a UI/UX designer who asked to be identified only as "Cat," speculated to The Register about the reasons for the alleged hack and Discord ban. "Our model, NovaSpark, is a good deal ahead of Comma's latest small and large models, which directly threatens their core business of making AI models good enough to sell their hardware," he said. "Comma for the most part has been stagnant in their models' improvement and that was a main driver for us making NovaSpark." An October 7, 2026 Discord message from user Torq_boi, said to be Harald Schäfer, Comma.ai’s CTO, implies NovaSpark was distilled from Comma.ai's Rebellious Hope model. “I’m glad people are training models and experimenting with this stuff," the post starts. "But don’t lie to people about what you’re doing, and saying it’s not a finetune of existing comma models when it is. That’s not cool.” IQ.Lvbs disputes that assertion and says it did the work on its own. "The claim that NovaSpark is Rebellious Hope with a short fine-tune and an unchanged policy does not survive scrutiny, and we’re not sure how Comma came to that conclusion, especially considering that they do not possess NovaSpark’s model weights or ONNX," the biz said. In the log data IQ.Lvbs published to support its claims, the company flags the username haraschax as one of those associated with Comma.ai IP addresses. Schäfer uses that username on GitHub. Comma.ai and Schäfer did not respond to requests for comment sent to several different addresses. The Discord user Torq_boi in the Comma.ai channel did not respond to a DM seeking comment. Comma.ai is currently being investigated [PDF] by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to assess whether its driving automation tech contributed to five crashes and three deaths. item.title: Cops raid office of RFK Jr. allies planning “unethical” vaccine trial on babies
item.description: Police in Guinea-Bissau raided the offices of Danish researchers on Monday, seizing doses of hepatitis B vaccine intended for a vaccine trial for newborns. International health experts have called the trial " unethical ," but anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has attempted to fund it with US taxpayer dollars. Under Kennedy, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced in December that it had awarded the Danish researchers—led by married couple Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project— an unsolicited $1.6 million grant to run the trial . Aaby and Stabell Benn are controversial vaccine researchers who claim vaccines cause overlooked harms. They have been repeatedly praised by Kennedy, but are currently under investigation for alleged scientific misconduct by Danish authorities. Plans for the trial were halted in January as widespread condemnation erupted over the trial's design, which would potentially expose thousands of newborns in the country to hepatitis B, risking a lifelong infection that can lead to liver cirrhosis, cancer, and premature death. Outrage flared again after a Rolling Stone story earlier this month claimed the CDC set aside another $1.6 million in funding in late September and planned to move forward with the trial. Read full article Comments

item.title: Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
item.description: Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter's third quarter earnings call Tuesday . Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of independent directors (though he did not name them). He also noted that he is not a member of either committee, nor involved in any of the discussions. "Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees," Musk said. "So it's an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can't be in the conversation. … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Microsoft reportedly projects $1,200 to $1,800 price for 2028 Project Helix
item.description: We haven't heard many details about Microsoft's upcoming "Project Helix" gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will "play your Xbox and PC games." In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma , though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with "a next-generation handheld device" planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800. That future console price range is based on what has "internally been projected" at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if "Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost," the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past . While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation , it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore's Law and AI-driven component shortages mean cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn't as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price , while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900 , and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750 . Read full article Comments

item.title: Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
item.description: Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. item.title: Tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs sit idle in Meta's Prometheus supercluster, just waiting for a failure
item.description: More than 11 percent of the GPUs at Meta’s Prometheus supercluster in New Albany, Ohio, are either dead or sitting idle waiting to step in when the next drops out, Zuckercorp revealed this week. The massive pool of redundant GPUs is just one of several measures the hyperscaler has taken to keep its AI training runs on track. Prometheus is among Meta's largest compute deployments to date. Powered by Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and (soon) Vera Rubin rack systems, Meta says the supercluster will eventually scale to a gigawatt of capacity spanning about a million accelerators. But as anyone who has worked on a large scale compute cluster understands, whether for LLM training or traditional HPC workloads, more chips inevitably means more problems. In an eight-GPU node, the chance of having a GPU fail is relatively low. In a 100,000-GPU cluster, failures are unavoidable. Meta is building something that's 10x larger and requires distributed training runs across multiple datacenters. Keeping the entire thing humming long enough to reach the next checkpoint becomes a major headache. In a blog post published this week, Meta offered a unique look at the work it's done to keep failures from derailing the development of models like Muse Spark or its most recent release Muse Wonder. Idle GPUs are the cost of continuity When Meta began the first phase of its Prometheus deployment in New Albany, the company says, it was experiencing roughly 1,000 interruptions per day for every 8,000 GPUs. Interruptions don't mean GPU failure. They simply mean something crashed, failed, or timed out, forcing the training run to stop and roll back to the last known good checkpoint. Meta claims in the year since it's been able to cut down the number of interruptions by 99 percent, to about 11 per day per 8,000 GPUs. One of the ways it's done this is by keeping some of Prometheus' GPUs in reserve. The cluster is currently powered by a combination of GB200 and GB300 systems, each with 72 GPUs per NVLink domain. However, only 64 of them are ever in use at any given moment. The other eight are essentially hot spares. Meta did this because a single failed GPU would take out an entire rack and interrupt the training run. Now, when a GPU fails, one of the spares can slot in and take its place. While this saves time — Meta doesn't have to drop the entire rack from the cluster or wait for someone to swap the faulty component to start training again — a failed GPU would still result in an interruption, albeit a shorter one. Parallel resiliency To mitigate this, Meta took advantage of the fact that large scale training jobs usually use data parallelism, where multiple copies of the model are resident within the cluster. "When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training," Meta explained. item.dc:creator: Tobias Mann
item.content:encoded: More than 11 percent of the GPUs at Meta’s Prometheus supercluster in New Albany, Ohio, are either dead or sitting idle waiting to step in when the next drops out, Zuckercorp revealed this week. The massive pool of redundant GPUs is just one of several measures the hyperscaler has taken to keep its AI training runs on track. Prometheus is among Meta's largest compute deployments to date. Powered by Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and (soon) Vera Rubin rack systems, Meta says the supercluster will eventually scale to a gigawatt of capacity spanning about a million accelerators. But as anyone who has worked on a large scale compute cluster understands, whether for LLM training or traditional HPC workloads, more chips inevitably means more problems. In an eight-GPU node, the chance of having a GPU fail is relatively low. In a 100,000-GPU cluster, failures are unavoidable. Meta is building something that's 10x larger and requires distributed training runs across multiple datacenters. Keeping the entire thing humming long enough to reach the next checkpoint becomes a major headache. In a blog post published this week, Meta offered a unique look at the work it's done to keep failures from derailing the development of models like Muse Spark or its most recent release Muse Wonder. Idle GPUs are the cost of continuity When Meta began the first phase of its Prometheus deployment in New Albany, the company says, it was experiencing roughly 1,000 interruptions per day for every 8,000 GPUs. Interruptions don't mean GPU failure. They simply mean something crashed, failed, or timed out, forcing the training run to stop and roll back to the last known good checkpoint. Meta claims in the year since it's been able to cut down the number of interruptions by 99 percent, to about 11 per day per 8,000 GPUs. One of the ways it's done this is by keeping some of Prometheus' GPUs in reserve. The cluster is currently powered by a combination of GB200 and GB300 systems, each with 72 GPUs per NVLink domain. However, only 64 of them are ever in use at any given moment. The other eight are essentially hot spares. Meta did this because a single failed GPU would take out an entire rack and interrupt the training run. Now, when a GPU fails, one of the spares can slot in and take its place. While this saves time — Meta doesn't have to drop the entire rack from the cluster or wait for someone to swap the faulty component to start training again — a failed GPU would still result in an interruption, albeit a shorter one. Parallel resiliency To mitigate this, Meta took advantage of the fact that large scale training jobs usually use data parallelism, where multiple copies of the model are resident within the cluster. "When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training," Meta explained. "The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput." In other words, Meta's training runs only get interrupted if the fault exceeds the data parallel domain. When this happens, the company has implemented a comprehensive checkpointing scheme, which you can think of a bit like auto-save or a revision history. That way if something does fail, Meta doesn't have to start over from scratch. "Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage," the company wrote. NVLink growing pains Meta says one of the most difficult challenges was making the NVLink fabrics used to connect 72 GPUs behave like one great big accelerator. Earlier H100 and H200-based systems featured just eight GPUs per NVLink domain, which meant the links were far shorter and less numerous. But this functionality was expanded nine-fold with Nvidia's Blackwell generation. "With over 600,000 NVLink connections, even marginal signal degradation triggers frequent NVLink recovery cycles," the company wrote. To overcome this, Meta had to implement a continuous telemetry system and conduct L11 diagnostic burns to isolate weak links before the systems were put into production. Power was another challenge. Ramping up and down tens of thousands of GPUs for a training run can introduce massive spikes in power consumption called transients, which can overwhelm power supply equipment. According to Meta, by focusing on the stability and reliability of its cluster, it was able to achieve more than 85 percent "goodput" — a measure of useful throughput — for pretraining and more than 90 percent for reinforcement learning on its latest model Muse Wonder. The company's ambitions don't stop here. As it works its way toward a million GPUs, Meta hopes to get its interruption rate down to just two per day for every 8,000 GPUs, or about 100,000 GPU-hours mean time between interrupts. ®

item.title: Oura adds two new cardiovascular health tracking features to its smart rings
item.description: Oura is introducing two new cardiovascular-focused health tracking features to its smart rings designed to help users better understand the effect regular workouts and exercise are having on their long-term health, and whether they need to ramp it up or dial things down. Cardio Effort and automatic VO2 Max (previously known as Cardio Capacity ) are available for the Oura Ring Gen 3 and later models , but only to users with an active Oura membership . Instead of measuring how fast or far a user went during a run or bike ride, or metrics like calories burned, Cardio Effort measures how hard their cardiovascular system was working during exercise … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: JustWatch, which tackles streaming fragmentation, launches own streaming service
item.description: Since launching in 2015, JustWatch has helped people navigate the growing number of streaming services by providing a guide on where to find movies they want to stream. Now JustWatch has its own streaming service and wants people to subscribe. Launched today, JustWatch TV offers some movies available for free with ads that aren’t free on any other streaming service, including Green Room (2015), Locke (2013), and Sing Sing (2023). Other free movies include Fiddlin ’ (2018 ), Friday the 13th (1980), and Hotel Mumbai (2018). I could play movies available for free on JustWatch TV without creating an account. JustWatch TV also has movies you can rent. Read full article Comments

item.title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash
item.description: Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30. Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page. A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy rollout. In response to backlash, Meta's spokesperson provided a statement to Ars, acknowledging Nieman Lab's initial report but not its follow-up report reiterating experts' concerns: Read full article Comments

item.title: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
item.description: Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn't available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature. As Google points out , a generative AI's outputs are better "when it knows the world and knows you," which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don't have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar. Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, "Google built-in" is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it's the other way around. Read full article Comments

item.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
item.description: Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet. As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices. One word: bonkers The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here - Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide. Read full article Comments

item.title: TP-Link tries to appease Trump admin with pledge to assemble routers in US
item.description: TP-Link yesterday announced plans to assemble Wi-Fi routers in the US, as the company attempts to get the Trump administration's approval to sell its newest routers to American consumers. The timing is uncertain, as TP-Link's press release said it expects US-based assembly to begin "as early as" 2027. TP-Link's application to sell new routers in the US could be rejected by the Trump administration or remain pending long enough to push the US-based assembly to 2028. "Pending US regulatory approval, TP-Link expects domestic assembly of its groundbreaking Wi-Fi 8 home networking product line to begin as early as next year," the company said. TP-Link said it signed a Letter of Intent with US company Keytronic, which agreed "to become a primary domestic manufacturing partner for TP-Link, supporting assembly of the company’s advanced networking portfolio in Corinth, Mississippi." Read full article Comments

item.title: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
item.description: It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation. The initial 100-series variant of the Antares rocket was kind of a hot mess. The rocket used old Soviet engines built during the era when Apollo astronauts were landing on the Moon. Decades later, in the 1990s, Aerojet acquired the engines and refurbished them for a rocket that would launch in the 2010s. Predictably, on the fifth launch of an Antares rocket in 2014, it exploded. The Antares vehicle is the last of a dying breed of medium-lift rockets—defined as having a lift capacity of 2 to 20 metric tons—in the United States. Nearly a decade and a half later there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine. Read full article Comments

item.title: Ukraine’s drone rescue of wounded soldier puts much touted idea into practice
item.description: Ukraine’s unprecedented drone rescue of a wounded soldier from the battlefield has shown once again how battlefield necessity can spur innovation. The operation was revealed just days after separate Ukrainian drones designed for casualty evacuation were deployed for frontline testing—taking a step beyond the US military’s decades of experimentation with similar concepts. The drone evacuation of the injured soldier took place at an undisclosed time and place on the frontline where the presence of Russian drones and landmines made it impractical to send in a wheeled ground robot , according to The Kyiv Independent . On October 19, Ukraine’s Army shared a video of the drone evacuation, showing the wounded soldier securing himself in a harness suspended beneath a heavy hexacopter drone with six rotors before being flown to safety. “This is a historic event, the next stage of evacuating the wounded, which we will all come to,” said Napalm, a programmer of the 92nd separate assault brigade's unmanned ground systems company, who went by his callsign per Ukrainian military practice, in a statement. “Now the serious systematic work begins, so that such missions are carried out constantly.” Read full article Comments

item.title: Quantum error correction goes well beyond breakeven
item.description: Running complicated algorithms on quantum computing hardware is going to require the use of logical qubits, where collections of hardware qubits are linked together in ways that allow errors to be detected and corrected. In general, the more hardware qubits you dedicate to each logical qubit, the better the chances are of identifying errors. But, given that the hardware qubits are prone to errors, adding more of them also increases the probability that errors will occur. If the hardware error rate is too high, then growing the logical qubit will only make matters worse. Fortunately, several companies have demonstrated hardware where the error rate is not too high. Several demonstrations show logical qubits are beyond the breakeven point, where adding more qubits improves performance. The problem is that the improvement isn't very dramatic. To lower error rates to levels we'll need to run complex algorithms, we'd have to add a completely impractical number of qubits to each logical qubit. On Monday, Quantinuum announced that its current generation of hardware is capable of scaling well beyond the breakeven point. Each step up in the size of logical qubits improved some measures of their performance by a factor of over 10. Read full article Comments

item.title: Meta tries to scapegoat staff who downloaded torrents to spare execs
item.description: In copyright lawsuits over AI training, Meta has spent weeks blaming staff for downloading torrents. The company has now been ordered to name executives who authorized decisions to pirate books from shadow libraries like Anna’s Archive and LibGen, TorrentFreak reported . In a discovery order impacting a class action raised by book authors—including Richard Kadrey and Sarah Silverman—as well as a lawsuit from publisher Entrepreneur Media, Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixon largely agreed that Meta must clearly identify key decision-makers. Following testimony from Meta staff who downloaded torrents, the order could expose a wider range of supervisors, managers, and executives whom staffers said greenlit the piracy. Meta had been hoping to avoid detailing the chain of command, particularly for leadership involved in early AI training. According to a Meta court filing , its initial efforts to compile massive AI datasets were managed through an “informal approach" where supposedly nobody with authority made any decisions. Instead, Meta insisted that a “decision” was “made only in the sense” that some staffers “technically” downloaded torrents. Read full article Comments

According to a Meta court filing , its initial efforts to compile massive AI datasets were managed through an “informal approach" where supposedly nobody with authority made any decisions. Instead, Meta insisted that a “decision” was “made only in the sense” that some staffers “technically” downloaded torrents. Read full article Comments

item.title: Palo Alto's firewall OS has been under attack from multiple ransomware groups since June
item.description: Multiple ransomware groups, including Qilin and Inc, have been exploiting a high-severity authentication bypass bug in Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS, with Unit 42 investigating attacks since early June across numerous industries, such as finance, healthcare, and manufacturing. CVE-2026-0257 affects PAN-OS GlobalProtect portals and gateways, potentially allowing attackers to bypass security restrictions and establish an unauthorized VPN connection. The security vendor first disclosed and patched the bug on May 13 and initially assigned it a medium-severity rating, saying it was aware of attempts to exploit it but had not observed any malicious exploitation. That assessment quickly changed, and by the end of the month, Rapid7 researchers said they observed successful exploitation across multiple customer environments dating back to at least May 17. On Monday, Palo Alto Networks’ consulting and incident response biz, Unit 42, said ransomware crews including Qilin and Inc continue to batter the CVE. “Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session,” said Andy Piazza, a senior director of threat intelligence at Unit 42. After gaining initial access, the criminals move laterally across the networks using Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block (SMB), dropping additional malware for credential harvesting and data theft before ultimately deploying ransomware, Piazza warned. In its ongoing investigations, Unit 42 has spotted the ransomware criminals infecting “numerous industries, including education, financial services, healthcare, high tech, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and wholesale and retail." Palo Alto Networks did not respond to The Register ’s inquiries about the attacks, including how many organizations have been infected. Additionally, ReliaQuest intel analysts warned that “multiple threat groups,” including Settra ransomware operators , are also exploiting the bug to gain initial access to corporate networks via unauthorized VPN sessions. “The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer,” Piazza wrote. “In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).” This allows the miscreants to bypass in-guest endpoint detection and response products, and represents “a highly sophisticated method” of stealing domain-wide credentials, he added. Unit 42 has also spotted criminals chaining this exploit for initial access with other vulner

item.title: ‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providers
item.description: Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say It happened again. A power outage hit a datacentre in London , and things cascaded from there: multiple banking services faltered, court hearings were put on hold and patients reported temporary glitches on the NHS app. The datacentre in question was in Google’s europe-west2-b zone, one of more than a dozen “zones” that the US search giant maintains in Europe to service its clients. item.title: Swamped curl maintainers take low-level flaws public to survive vulnerability 'avalanche'
item.description: An "avalanche of vulnerability reports" is forcing curl to move lower-severity cases into public view, reserving private handling for high and critical flaws. From October 26, low and medium-severity reports should be filed in the open source data transfer tool's public GitHub repository, maintainer Daniel Stenberg said . "Security researchers in doubt can still submit the issue on HackerOne and we can tell them what severity we deem it to be. Over the last few years, over 90 percent of all submissions could quickly be assessed to be less than HIGH." Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty scheme this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team. Stenberg has previously acknowledged that not all AI-assisted reports are bad, but the workload now demands another response. "This policy change is entirely triggered by the current avalanche of vulnerability reports that keep pouring in . We see no end to them and we do not anticipate this flood to decrease within the next several months. "We are struggling as a project as all key maintainers feel strained, overloaded and brought to the brink of what we can muster. We must act to survive. This is our next step in a survival strategy. It might not be our last. We aim to not drown." Public handling would let more people assess reports, develop fixes, write advisories, and check for related problems before releases ship, Stenberg said. Handling vulnerability reports publicly won't reduce the work per report, he admits, though it could spread the load and make the resulting lessons and documentation easier to find. At least that's the theory. Public disclosure also gives attackers more time to exploit flaws before fixes arrive. The maintainer agrees this is unfortunate yet unavoidable. "We limit this practice to less than HIGH for this reason: at least these problems are not terrible." Stenberg said researchers using AI are generating unusual option combinations unlikely to occur in real applications, then treating minor discrepancies as vulnerabilities. "We can't continue down this spiraling path with our sanity intact. We don't have the bandwidth, manpower or even will to handle a never-ending vulnerability reporting stream at this pace. I believe few software projects can stand this kind of prolonged high volume deluge for extended periods. Something needs to give way." ®

item.title: OneDrive loses bunch of Copilot shortcuts in File Explorer clear-out
item.description: Microsoft is pruning OneDrive's Copilot options from File Explorer's right-click menu, though the AI assistant isn't being shown the door entirely. The Windows giant will remove shortcuts for summarizing documents, generating FAQs, comparing files and images, explaining images, extracting text, and asking questions. The rollout begins in mid-November and is expected to finish by early December. "Ask Copilot" will remain. Microsoft's September 2025 announcement of the feature said: "We are bringing the power of AI directly into your daily file management experience. With just a few clicks, Copilot can help you summarize lengthy documents, generate an FAQ, compare files, or answer questions about your file." Users can still right-click a OneDrive file and select "Ask Copilot" to start a conversation with the file attached, or use the Copilot icon in File Explorer Home. The individual actions will also remain available in the OneDrive activity center. Adding a clutch of Copilot options with identical icons did little to make an already crowded menu easier to navigate. In its message on the subject, Microsoft said: "We're simplifying how people use Copilot with their OneDrive files in File Explorer." An extra click, yes, but at least you won't need a taller screen to view even more context menu options. Microsoft has stated that it intends to adopt a more thoughtful approach to how and where its AI assistant turns up in its product line. In March 2026, Windows boss Pavan Davuluri said : "We are reducing unnecessary Copilot entry points." File Explorer's crowded right-click menu seems as good a place to start as any. The File Explorer context menu is also undergoing an overhaul as part of Microsoft's attempt to make it less "cluttered and sluggish," to the point where users could opt to have it work a bit like it used to in Windows 10. ®

item.title: openEuler brings China's enterprise Linux ambitions to the desktop
item.description: Surprisingly few organizations were promoting Linux distros at Open Source Summit Europe. The only dedicated stands we found belonged to two Chinese projects, with openEuler occupying the larger booth. For users accustomed to Western enterprise distros, openEuler may be a less familiar name, but it has an impressive history. It's the modern free community version of Huawei's EulerOS, a version of which achieved official official UNIX™ certification . openEuler is no longer a solely Huawei project, though. Since then, it's been opened up, and it is now run by the OpenAtom Foundation . OpenAtom was co-founded in 2020 by Huawei along with some other big Chinese names, such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent. Another of the co-founders was Inspur, which formerly developed its own distro, K/UX – a version of which also achieved official UNIX™ certification . Inspur K/UX won Unix certification in February 2016, and EulerOS seven months later. K/UX's Unix certification expired in 2019. A few months later, in May 2019, the US placed wider sanctions on Huawei . It is possible that the fresh restrictions on American sales prompted Huawei's interest in closer co-operation with other companies in the Chinese Linux space. As far as we can see, there were no further versions of K/UX after version 3. As additional motivation for cooperation, both EulerOS and K/UX were originally based on CentOS Linux, and of course, in December 2020, the CentOS Project announced it would shift its focus from CentOS Linux to CentOS Stream . The openEuler community has taken the platform in new directions. It has built its own stack of tools for developing, deploying, and running LLMs, called Intelligence BooM . It has a tool for migrating CentOS Linux systems to openEuler, called x2openEuler . As you would expect, it supports Kubernetes, as well as Docker and Podman, but it also has its own container engine called iSula (named after a species of ant ). Aware that it's less known outside Asia, at the Open Source Summit, OpenAtom was handing out copies of a special "Focus Guide" from Admin Magazine, which is also available as a free download . Some parts of this are also available online without registration, such as AI and the BooM Stack and Automating Migration to openEuler . openEuler has a dual-strand release cycle , akin to Ubuntu rather than the RHELatives, with LTS versions and more frequent "innovation releases." The current LTS is version 24.03, released in June 2024 , while the latest version is 26.09. There is a plethora of versions and editions available on the downloads page : the latest release is for x86-64 and 64-bit Arm. The LTS version adds support for RISC-V and LoongArch, and there are minimal versions for 32-bit Arm as well. The older 22.03 LTS was also available for SW-64, meaning the SunWay RISC processors that Register sister site The Next Platform looked at in 2016. As LWN put it last year , this is a "non-upstream kernel port." There are five types of install
item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: Surprisingly few organizations were promoting Linux distros at Open Source Summit Europe. The only dedicated stands we found belonged to two Chinese projects, with openEuler occupying the larger booth. For users accustomed to Western enterprise distros, openEuler may be a less familiar name, but it has an impressive history. It's the modern free community version of Huawei's EulerOS, a version of which achieved official official UNIX™ certification . openEuler is no longer a solely Huawei project, though. Since then, it's been opened up, and it is now run by the OpenAtom Foundation . OpenAtom was co-founded in 2020 by Huawei along with some other big Chinese names, such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent. Another of the co-founders was Inspur, which formerly developed its own distro, K/UX – a version of which also achieved official UNIX™ certification . Inspur K/UX won Unix certification in February 2016, and EulerOS seven months later. K/UX's Unix certification expired in 2019. A few months later, in May 2019, the US placed wider sanctions on Huawei . It is possible that the fresh restrictions on American sales prompted Huawei's interest in closer co-operation with other companies in the Chinese Linux space. As far as we can see, there were no further versions of K/UX after version 3. As additional motivation for cooperation, both EulerOS and K/UX were originally based on CentOS Linux, and of course, in December 2020, the CentOS Project announced it would shift its focus from CentOS Linux to CentOS Stream . The openEuler community has taken the platform in new directions. It has built its own stack of tools for developing, deploying, and running LLMs, called Intelligence BooM . It has a tool for migrating CentOS Linux systems to openEuler, called x2openEuler . As you would expect, it supports Kubernetes, as well as Docker and Podman, but it also has its own container engine called iSula (named after a species of ant ). Aware that it's less known outside Asia, at the Open Source Summit, OpenAtom was handing out copies of a special "Focus Guide" from Admin Magazine, which is also available as a free download . Some parts of this are also available online without registration, such as AI and the BooM Stack and Automating Migration to openEuler . openEuler has a dual-strand release cycle , akin to Ubuntu rather than the RHELatives, with LTS versions and more frequent "innovation releases." The current LTS is version 24.03, released in June 2024 , while the latest version is 26.09. There is a plethora of versions and editions available on the downloads page : the latest release is for x86-64 and 64-bit Arm. The LTS version adds support for RISC-V and LoongArch, and there are minimal versions for 32-bit Arm as well. The older 22.03 LTS was also available for SW-64, meaning the SunWay RISC processors that Register sister site The Next Platform looked at in 2016. As LWN put it last year , this is a "non-upstream kernel port." There are five types of installation ISO available: Offline Standard, Offline Everything (a hefty 24.9 GB), Network Install (a still significant 1.5 GB), and two variants of the desktop "DevStation" version – a basic one at 3.3 GB and an "everything" edition at 25 GB. We gave the DevStation a very quick whirl in VirtualBox. It boots into its own installation program called Heolleo , which offers the choice of Simplified Chinese or English. Installation took a while, as it automatically fetches updates as it goes. We ended up with a GNOME desktop configured for Chinese, but we opened Settings, typed "language" into the Search box, and picked English. After a reboot, we could read most of the desktop. Program groups and some other elements are still in Chinese, but it's navigable with a bit of guesswork. It's GNOME 49, with the Dash to Panel and Arc Menu extensions preinstalled for a slightly more familiar layout. Opening a terminal, we were greeted with: Welcome to 6.18.48-0.0.0.15.oe2609.x86_64 It also offers the Deepin Desktop Environment, UKUI (as seen in Ubuntu Kylin), MATE, Xfce, and the Kiran Desktop Environment , which is a new one to us. In places, the English-language materials for openEuler mention Chinese CPU makers rather than western ones – which is understandable, in context. Examples include processors from Hygon, a Chinese licensee of AMD designs , as well as Phytium and Kunpeng , which explain the Arm support on offer. In the western world, the Red Hat user community responded to the end of CentOS Linux by building new free distros that stay as close as they can to their progenitor: the Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux projects , rebuilt from Red Hat source code. Then, when the IBM subsidiary restricted access to that source to its customers in 2023, the Rocky and AlmaLinux projects started to diverge. Rocky aims for the closest possible RHEL compatibility, and its most visible innovation is that it's built its own new build service . It also found a clever workaround to get Red Hat's kernel source code. AlmaLinux still targets RHEL compatibility, but differentiates itself by retaining older device support and older CPU architectures after Red Hat drops them. Chinese vendors have responded very differently. Those offering CentOS Linux-based OSes clubbed together, dropped their rival versions and their UNIX compatibility efforts, and instead are working on new tools and subsystems. Much like European interest in digital sovereignty , this is in part due to the Trump administration. Half a decade after it was cut off from its upstream sources, the openEuler platform is thriving and growing, even if few in the western world pay any attention at all. ®

item.title: How going dual-native means VM/container co-existence and sovereign security in the AI era
item.description: Seasoned techies recall with nostalgia a simpler time when the “single-stack” model of enterprise computing held as the default approach to solving interoperability headaches. Back then IT decision-makers were prepared to forfeit some choice and flexibility in how they specified IT systems in return for the availability and manageability that came with a homogenous operating environment. With the subsequent rise of multi-clouds, application-specific hardware, ever-changing business requirements, and the race for AI, the old “one-size-fits-all” playbook has been largely abandoned. Most IT estates have embraced technological diversity, some by design, some through standardization, some by inertia. Modern enterprise environments have become innately heterogeneous – and innately complex. They run a diverse combo of system software, hardware devices, cloud services, legacy applications, et al . The advance of AI has brought standard CPUs, specialized GPUs, fast networking fabrics, distributed data pipelines, and new deployment models that span private clouds, public clouds, edge – and ever-pressing ROI expectations. But that doesn’t mean that companies’ existing applications and data simply disappear. One trying but inevitable outcome of rapid AI deployment is the so-called “VM-container divide”. This is where critical business applications tipped to transition to containers continue to run on virtual machines, because cloud-native services are taking precedence, nabbing container and Kubernetes availability. So companies face the challenge of operationalizing AI, without being forced into complex migrations or creating new infrastructure silos. Dealing with this technological schism poses acute challenges for IT management. Many new AI deployments are going straight to containers, while existing data and applications – which the AI needs to access – continue to run on VMs. Running separate stacks for VMs and containers creates a number of issues, such as duplicate capacity plans, separate support contracts, and fragmented governance. And after years of trying to get beyond the pitfalls of siloed data, exasperated enterprises are now having to deal with siloed infrastructure. Separately managed VM and container environments often mean inefficient resource utilization. This in turn can lead to “stranded capacity” – installed computing resources that cannot be used to support live workloads. VM clusters are frequently underutilized while container pools (like Kubernetes) are overprovisioned, with no easy way to share resources without manual intervention. Furthermore, VM/container infrastructure fragmentation can create an operations bottleneck for agentic AI. Infrastructure fragmentation can complicate the deployment, integration, governance, and scaling of agents thus making it harder to operationalize and scale agentic AI securely and consistently. Infrastructure fragmentation can complicate the deployment, integration, governance, and scaling of agents thus making it harder to operationalize and scale agentic AI securely and consistently. When AI agents cannot autonomously communicate across environments, their utility droops from autonomous problem-solvers to plain localised macros. Containers are gaining because of the widespread embrace of AI-enabled applications. Eighty-five percent of IT executives polled by Nutanix’s most recent Enterprise Cloud Index survey think that AI is accelerating their organization’s adoption of containers in a meaningful way; 29 percent think it is speeding-up adoption “to a great extent”. “AI is accelerating the shift to containers because machine learning models require strict dependency packing, while critical applications and data remain spread across both virtualised and containerised environments,” says Harsha Kotikela, Senior Director of Product & Solutions Marketing at Nutanix. Agents are multi-tier by nature he explains. “Inference is typically GPU-intensive and container-based, while agents are often CPU-intensive and container-based, and existing enterprise applications and data largely remain in VM environments. The challenge is to bring these tiers together so agents can work with enterprise applications and data, without forcing migration or creating additional infrastructure silos.” The application landscape, meanwhile, has become just as diverse. Many organisations simultaneously operate traditional enterprise applications running on VMs, containerised apps, distributed AI applications and intelligent agents, with workloads deployed across private cloud, public cloud, and edge. Each environment has its own management tools, operational processes, security rules and governance models. “Management capability has struggled to scale up commensurately,” says Kotikela, but adding more consoles or building separate operational teams for every technology stack does not necessarily solve this complexity: “In many cases, it increases it.” However, Kotikela challenges the notion that the predicament enterprises face in straddling the VM-container divide is intractable. Rather, the challenge is to move towards a unified operating model that allows them to operationalize agentic AI while retaining flexibility across their existing and new environments. “Rather than trying to work around heterogeneity, the objective now should be to make heterogeneous environments operate consistently with purposeful policies,” Kotikela says. “This is where Nutanix's dual-native architecture comes in, enabling enterprises to operationalize agentic AI across container-based inference and agent workloads alongside existing VM-based applications and data, through a consistent operating model.” The reality is that the VM-to-container migration trend is sluggish, Kotikela suggests. Few enterprises are starting from scratch with containers. Many have long-established business applications on legacy architectures, on top of which they are building container-based applications, but mostly not to replace what they already have running on VMs. Rather, they are prolonging their VM investment. It’s customer interest that’s informed how Nutanix provisions a governed, dual-native architecture through its Nutanix Cloud Platform – NCP – which runs traditional VMs and containerised/Kubernetes-based AI workloads concurrently on a single, consistent infrastructure. NCP’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure foundation unifies compute, storage, virtualisation and management across on-premises resources, public clouds and edge. It works in concert with Nutanix Enterprise AI (NAI), which provides the software capabilities to deploy, govern, and scale AI workloads. Technology partnerships are vital to building AI support functionality into Nutanix's AI portfolio, explains Kotikela. “Nutanix and NVIDIA work together to provide an integrated platform for enterprise AI, combining Nutanix’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure and software with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI software. Nutanix Enterprise AI simplifies the deployment, management, and secure operation of AI models, integrating with NVIDIA NIM and NeMo microservices to support enterprise AI inference and agentic AI workflows.” Meanwhile, “Nutanix Kubernetes Platform provides the foundation for managing Kubernetes environments, while Nutanix Unified Storage delivers the high-performance data access required by AI workloads. Together, these capabilities help enterprises deploy and scale AI while maintaining control over their infrastructure, models, and data.” Stacks of opportunity “In an ideal IT world you do not want to have to manage two different operational stacks – but the world of IT is rarely ‘ideal’,” Kotikela points out. “So you have to approach the challenge from a realistic perspective. You cannot bend your current stacks to a different reality without the risk of something breaking, and there’s no sense in that.” He adds: “A platform that unifies VMs and containers improves developer time-to-value by getting rid of those infrastructure silos, and providing a single control plane.” Rather than development teams having to manage separate pipelines for existing VMs and

item.title: Polestar tries to quantify what it’s like to drive a performance car
item.description: The human desire to go fast is old, dating back at least as far as the first time some adventurous Yamnaya saw a horse on the Pontic-Caspian steppe and thought, “I bet if I jumped on that thing’s back, it would be faster than walking.” A thousand years later, someone else invented the wheel—and the chariot—and humanity was ready to roll. Now, about five millennia since that first horseback ride, equestrianism is mostly a leisure activity, and we drive cars, propelled by motors with more power than an entire herd of beasts could muster. Acceleration, top speed, and lap times are the usual ways we quantify that performance, and performance electric vehicles are currently in an arms race to see which one can hit 60 mph in the least amount of time. But measuring a car’s performance is easy—all you need is a stopwatch and a track. How about measuring the effect of car performance on the driver? That’s a question Polestar is trying to answer with researchers at the University of Oxford. Read full article Comments

item.title: Enterprises blow nearly a third of software budgets on upgrades they never asked for
item.description: Enterprises say nearly a third of their software budgets goes on upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes they wouldn't have chosen, according to research suggesting that keeping vendors happy has become an expensive business. The study , conducted by Censuswide for software support provider Origina and published with Thinkers50, surveyed 2,018 senior IT decision-makers in the US and UK. Respondents put the average share at 28 percent. And customers aren't necessarily getting anything better for their money. Some 95 percent of respondents said they had paid for at least one vendor-driven change in the past three years despite expecting worse reliability, performance, or value. The most recent vendor-driven change cost respondents' organizations an average of $12.87 million. Origina calls this the "software tax," but unlike most taxes, it comes with the added pleasure of potentially making your IT systems worse. The costs don't stop at software either. According to the survey, 91 percent of respondents said their organizations had retired working hardware in the past three years to meet software support deadlines, sacrificing an estimated 1.65 years of remaining useful life on average. Then there's the small matter of finding people to carry out all these supposedly essential changes. Some 84 percent said experienced engineers were regularly diverted from other projects to handle vendor-driven upgrades and migrations. That leaves less time for the work businesses actually want done, including the AI projects that software vendors themselves have spent the past few years telling everyone they urgently need. Asked about the last time an AI or data project was delayed, paused, or canceled, 90 percent said vendor-driven costs contributed at least moderately. While customers might be tempted to tell their suppliers where to stick their next upgrade, many apparently don't feel they have much choice. Some 76 percent said they have little negotiating leverage with their major software vendors. Origina founder and CEO Tomás O'Leary reckons customers have been backed into a corner. "When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response. That's exactly the problem," he said. "The market has left some of the most experienced technology leaders in the world with little room to refuse, and that cost shows up in budgets, in engineering time and in innovation that never gets funded." The findings also suggest that IT bosses are getting rather fed up with the arrangement. Some 91 percent backed legislation that would give enterprise software customers protections comparable to those enjoyed by long-term residential tenants, while 82 percent supported software maintenance requirements similar to EU hardware repairability rules. item.title: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV
item.description: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy When Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.” Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasingly enshittified .” Continue reading...

item.title: The dangers of letting tech billionaires shape our world
item.description: As SpaceX impacts Ukraine and AI-generated music divides artists and fans, critics are asking what happens when technology has too much control over our lives This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while sitting in front of Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl, on view in New York City . Today in tech, we’re discussing the perils of Elon Musk’s one-man global infrastructure, AI-generated music and a Guardian AI conference in Paris. Continue reading...

item.title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
item.description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way. Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further. Continue reading...

item.title: HPE to launch AI straight to the Moon
item.description: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon. This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover. Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year. Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform. Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole. What we know about SBC4 so far The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it. No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried. What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat. Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up. Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data. However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running. Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body. item.dc:creator: Tobias Mann
item.content:encoded: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon. This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover. Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year. Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform. Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole. What we know about SBC4 so far The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it. No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried. What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat. Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up. Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data. However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running. Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body. Not only do HPE’s systems power some of the fastest supercomputers on Earth, but they could soon hold the number one spot on the Moon — not that that’s a particularly high bar. Beyond bragging rights, a workload like HPL could have other benefits like helping to keep the rover from icing over during the roughly 14-day-long night cycles the rover will repeatedly endure over the course of its mission. Hardening SBC4 for the Moon The Rover and by extension SBC4 will have to contend with extreme vibration stresses during launch and landing, wild temperature swings, not to mention cosmic rays and solar radiation since the Moon lacks the thick atmosphere and magnetic field that shields terrestrial compute. But, as it turns out, radiation might not be as big a problem as you’d think. According to Fernandez, SBC4 is largely assembled from off-the-shelf components, including the solid state drives. The compute platform is using standard Kioxia BG6 M.2 drives with the main line of protection being a software RAID 1. “It’s a silent mirror. The boot order is to try this and if something has happened to it, go here,” Mark Fernandez, HPE’s chief scientist of space tech and solutions, explained. “With our nine years' experience in the Space Station using drives, we’ve even convinced them we don’t need to do anything special for space.” However, this wasn’t always the thinking. As we reported at the time, early Spaceborne Computers suffered from high SSD failure rates. But as it turned out, so did the same drives deployed terrestrially. The cause of the failures wasn’t cosmic rays or energetic particles from the Sun, but rather bad capacitors, he explained. “I’ve had zero SSD failure since 2019.” While off-the-shelf electronics are surprisingly radiation resistant — at least within FLIP’s mission parameters — HPE has invested heavily in software based redundancy and recovery. Fernandez calls this “hardware hardening in software.” The idea being that the spare CPU cycles are used to continuously monitor and compare hardware metrics against a state table. If a parameter exceeds the specified threshold, SBC4 will take action to protect itself. “At a high level, I say, I like to be running at full speed. I can't do that. I'll run at a slower speed. If I can't do that, I'd like to be booted, but not running anything, and then maybe the server will recover. And worst case, I'd like to be powered down rather than get destroyed,” he explained. At the edge of the edge FLIP is primarily intended as a proof of concept vehicle, which is to say it’s a test bed for technologies that may eventually find their way to the Moon on other missions. The inclusion of SBC4 reflects the realities of operating at the far edge of Earth’s orbit. The latency between Earth and the Moon is nowhere near as bad as Mars's up to 44 minute round-trip communication time, but even 2.5 seconds makes real-time control from Houston, or in this case Astrolab’s mission control, which by the way is also powered by HPE's Greenlake Private Cloud stack, in Hawthorne, California a bit unwieldy. Further complicating matters is the bandwidth afforded the rover. When Artemis 2 traveled around the Moon earlier this year, astronauts weren’t able to send back high-res photographs in real time due to the lack of bandwidth. It was only after the mission was on its way back to Earth that they were able to establish a big enough pipe to transmit the full-res images. For this reason, SBC4 is designed to operate “at the edge of the edge,” Fernandez said. Given the bandwidth constraints, it’s far easier to process as much of the data and telemetry gathered by the rover’s array of cameras, lidars, and environmental sensors locally. “It’s important to ship back insight to Earth rather than all the raw data whenever possible. So having the edge compute capability to process the raw data locally, save on bandwidth back to Earth,” Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews said. Matthews isn’t the only one to share this perspective. Earlier this year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the challenges and opportunities of space-based computing with analysts during the company’s Q1 earnings call. "There are many different computing problems that really want to be done in space," he said at the time. "One of the best use cases of GPUs in space is imaging. To be able to do imaging at very large, very high resolutions, extremely large scales and very, very fast, it's hard to do that by sending petabytes and petabytes of imaging data back here on Earth and doing that work, it's easier just to do it out in space." Though others' ambitions are far greater. Google, Amazon, and SpaceX are all touting orbital datacenters powered by the Sun as the answer to terrestrial power constraints — Elon Musk wants you to believe he'll eventually be manufacturing deep-space datacenters on the Moon and lobbing them into the far reaches of the solar system using mass drivers — the economics of getting those bit barns into low Earth orbit remain unproven and so far unviable. item.title: 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water
item.description: A test account protected by "Password1" helped an intruder steal personal data relating to 3,300 people, mostly children, in a ransomware attack that has drawn regulatory rebukes for two Welsh organizations. The Information Commission's Office (ICO) issued reprimands rather than fines to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, also known as Data Cymru. According to the ICO, altnet ONL provided server and connectivity infrastructure, licensing, and support to Data Cymru, which helps public bodies across Wales make effective use of data. On November 1, 2024, Data Cymru suffered a ransomware attack after a miscreant exploited a test account called Test2 to infiltrate its network and encrypt 182.7 GB of data housed in a file server and an internal database server. "Before deploying the ransomware, the threat actor exfiltrated 42 GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server," the ICO said on Tuesday in its reprimand of ONL [PDF]. ONL told the ICO it created the test account on January 13, 2012, during its initial project for Data Cymru. "ONL confirmed that the creation of the 'Test2' account was likely intended to test user account access before migrating 'real' users to its services," the ICO said. "When it was created, the 'Test2' account was given the password of 'Password1'." The ICO cited Bitwarden's password strength tool, which rated "Password1" as "very weak" and estimated a cracking time of less than a second. "The local administrator accounts on the three impacted systems all had the same password. This meant that once one system had been breached, the local account hashes could be collected and used by the threat actor to authenticate access to other systems on the Data Cymru network," the regulator added. "ONL confirmed that it did not carry out any reviews of local administrator accounts following their initial deployment. This meant these accounts remained active, regardless of whether they were used, and continued to use the same default passwords set at the time of their creation in January 2012, as part of ONL's initial project with Data Cymru, for more than 12.5 years." The data watchdog reprimanded ONL under Article 32 of the UK GDPR because it failed to put in place "appropriate technical and organisational measures" to ensure processing systems and services were safe, and it didn't regularly assess or evaluate those measures. It found ONL had no auditing procedures to review user accounts within Data Cymru's Active Directory. The ICO's separate reprimand of Data Cymru [PDF] also detailed failures in its security arrangements. "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors," said ICO head of investigations David Doodson. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands. "The responsibility for these failures
