Neither had put in place sufficiently clear and effective measures to ensure that old accounts were routinely identified and removed." ®

item.title: Google Cloud says a 'power event' caused today's outage
item.description: UPDATED Google Cloud has blamed a “power event” for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe, and is pledging to restore normal service within the hour. The unplanned downtime for customers began at 0608 UTC when europe-west-2-b, one of three local availability zones in the London region, started playing up. According to an update on its status page , Google Cloud said at 1158 UTC that full recovery workloads should be “completed, tentatively” by 1300 UTC. Customers can expect another update at that point, with Google either giving the thumbs up, thumbs sideways or having to admit engineers are still working on a fix. Services that went AWOL included BigQuery Data TransferService, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Managed Service for Apache Kafka. So what caused online services to melt at customers including Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Royal Mail, Rightmove, DPD, BT, Screwfix and Revolut? Power. "A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads." The Register has asked Google for further elucidation but it said the only information is available on the status page. The "fragility" of the cloud model is again on display, Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad , a lecturer in computer science at Keele University told The Register . He estimates that a total of 38 services were down and out for the count. "The incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures." "A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centered on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. True resilience requires designing for regional failures through multi-region deployments, workload portability, and tested disaster recovery procedures." item.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
item.description: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it's suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: Read full article Comments

item.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
item.description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...

item.title: Bullhorn sees red after cyberattack knocks recruitment platform offline
item.description: Bullhorn is the latest tech giant finding itself on the wrong end of a cyberattack, forcing the recruitment software provider to shut down its platform while it investigates. The US-based company, which serves more than 10,000 customers worldwide, says its systems are now back online in the UK, US, and Australia. Unfortunately for customers hoping to get back to work, online doesn't necessarily mean working. In its latest status update, published on Tuesday , Bullhorn confirmed that some users were still struggling with single sign-on (SSO), password resets, and customizations, while several products continued to report degraded performance. Things started going sideways on Friday, October 16, when Bullhorn flagged problems getting job postings onto Indeed. By the following morning, the platform was suffering a full-blown outage, and Bullhorn confirmed later that day that it was dealing with something rather more serious than a technical hiccup. "We have detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. We have temporarily disabled access to our systems in order to contain the activity while we investigate further," the company said, noting that it had roped in cybersecurity specialists from CrowdStrike to help investigate the attack and restore its services. For recruitment agencies using Bullhorn, the outage meant losing access to candidate records, job applications, placements and, in some cases, the systems used to get people paid. Services began returning on Monday, but recovery has been anything but seamless. As of Tuesday morning, Bullhorn's status page still listed degraded performance across several products, including its automation tools, Talent Platform, Onboarding365 and Time & Expense. While Bullhorn is making progress getting customers back into their accounts, it has yet to answer arguably the bigger question: whether the attackers stole anything. In its customer FAQ , it said a forensic investigation is ongoing, and has not yet determined whether attackers exfiltrated customer data. Bullhorn says it will contact affected customers if the investigation finds their information was compromised, and it also warned people to watch out for opportunistic crooks looking to exploit the chaos. "Threat actors may pose as Bullhorn personnel via email, text, or phone calls, using the incident as a pretext to request credentials or sensitive information," it warned on Tuesday, stressing that its employees would never ask customers to disclose passwords, multi-factor authentication codes, or verification tokens. The company has also required password resets for users who don’t log in through SSO, while customers using API integrations have been instructed to rotate their credentials. The cause of the intrusion remains unknown, and Bullhorn has not publicly identified the attackers or confirmed whether ransomware was involved. item.title: Microsoft admits that Always On VPN problems were not fixed in the October Security Update
item.description: Microsoft has been forced to admit that the Always On VPN glitch – which it said it had fixed in an update on October 13 – was not actually fixed after all. We've all been there. You fix that bug, or tweak the configuration setting, and you're pleased with yourself, but it turns out it didn't take, and you have to send the "er, about that fix" follow-up email of shame. The same has happened to Microsoft. After proudly declaring the problem resolved as part of its last security update , the company had to roll back its triumphant trumpeting to a sad little parp from a clown's horn in the message WI1482218: "This disclosure was mistakenly updated to Resolved status on October 13, 2026. We have returned its status to Mitigated. "We apologize for any inconvenience or confusion." The bug in question concerns the operating system's Always On VPN functionality, a useful bit of code that quietly opens a VPN connection in the background without tiresome prompts for authentication. It dates back to Windows 10, and Microsoft alerted administrators to problems after the September 2026 Windows security update inadvertently broke it. The issue affects Windows 11 versions from 24H2 through 26H2. The problem could occur when the VPN was set to try a different connection method if the initial connection failed (Microsoft gave the example of using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP). According to Microsoft: "Affected VPN connections might remain in a 'Connecting' state or repeatedly attempt to connect without succeeding. Subsequent connection attempts might also display the error: 'The specified port is already in use'." This is not ideal for administrators. The workaround Microsoft highlighted back on October 13 was to change from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, which would at least get affected users up and running. The workaround remains the same. The bad news is that, because last week's fix did not work, affected administrators will need to apply the workaround for a bit longer. Microsoft claimed, "A resolution for this issue is planned to be included in an update to be released in the coming weeks." ®

item.title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
item.description: As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips. Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even preorder a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit. Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is a bare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950 . It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Ars went for a ride in a Slate Truck over the summer , but we haven't had a chance to shop for one. So I stopped by the Slate Experience Center so I could, er, experience the Slate. Read full article Comments

item.title: Whitehall shuts the front door on digital ID but leaves the back open
item.description: Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure. Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans , officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are. The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing. But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates. That's quite a lot of paperwork for something that's supposedly dead. The revelations came during a Public Accounts Committee hearing on Monday, where MPs wanted to know what exactly had been scrapped. "But is it not the case, based on the answers you've given us this afternoon, that the infrastructure of digital ID in the public sector is still being pursued?" asked Sarah Green, Liberal Democrat MP for Chesham and Amersham. Susannah Storey, DCMS permanent secretary, was keen to draw a line between the national scheme ministers had scrapped and the digital identity projects Whitehall had no intention of abandoning. One Login already allows people to prove who they are online, she said, but "that is not the same as a national digital identity strategy." Rod Latham, DCMS director for cybersecurity and digital identity, had a convenient explanation for why so much of digital ID was still standing: the government had only scrapped plans for a new identity product. "We already had One Login and the Gov Wallet," he told MPs, adding that work on the digital identity trust framework was also underway before the national scheme was announced. Whitehall isn't wasting time putting that technology to use, with officials confirming that testing is already underway to enable digital credentials to work with private businesses. Natalie Jones, the senior responsible owner for GOV.UK One Login, revealed that the government had opened a testing environment for private sector providers to integrate with its digital wallet technology. This would let people use digital driving licenses to prove their age in pubs , collect parcels, or verify their identity online. "We've got a bit of a chicken and egg situation. A digital driving license is only useful if there are people ready and shops and businesses ready to receive it,” Jones said, noting that further testing is planned for December, with a national rollout of digital driving licenses targeted for 2027. item.dc:creator: Carly Page
item.content:encoded: Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure. Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans , officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are. The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing. But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates. That's quite a lot of paperwork for something that's supposedly dead. The revelations came during a Public Accounts Committee hearing on Monday, where MPs wanted to know what exactly had been scrapped. "But is it not the case, based on the answers you've given us this afternoon, that the infrastructure of digital ID in the public sector is still being pursued?" asked Sarah Green, Liberal Democrat MP for Chesham and Amersham. Susannah Storey, DCMS permanent secretary, was keen to draw a line between the national scheme ministers had scrapped and the digital identity projects Whitehall had no intention of abandoning. One Login already allows people to prove who they are online, she said, but "that is not the same as a national digital identity strategy." Rod Latham, DCMS director for cybersecurity and digital identity, had a convenient explanation for why so much of digital ID was still standing: the government had only scrapped plans for a new identity product. "We already had One Login and the Gov Wallet," he told MPs, adding that work on the digital identity trust framework was also underway before the national scheme was announced. Whitehall isn't wasting time putting that technology to use, with officials confirming that testing is already underway to enable digital credentials to work with private businesses. Natalie Jones, the senior responsible owner for GOV.UK One Login, revealed that the government had opened a testing environment for private sector providers to integrate with its digital wallet technology. This would let people use digital driving licenses to prove their age in pubs , collect parcels, or verify their identity online. "We've got a bit of a chicken and egg situation. A digital driving license is only useful if there are people ready and shops and businesses ready to receive it,” Jones said, noting that further testing is planned for December, with a national rollout of digital driving licenses targeted for 2027. MPs also pressed officials on privacy, particularly whether citizens would have to consent before their information was shared between government departments. "In the confines of digital ID used in digital services, then consent is the model," said Christine Bellamy, interim director general for digital products at the Government Digital Service. There's a catch, of course. Government departments can already share data without asking permission, and officials couldn't quite explain how that squares with their promises about consent. "The strategy needs to be fully finished," Bellamy admitted, which might not be the reassurance MPs were hoping for. Jones insisted that One Login was "not a big data lake," saying it stores identity information separately and cannot see what users do inside government services. "One Login does not issue a single identifier to people," she added. Rupert Lowe MP remained unconvinced, warning that Britain could end up getting digital ID "by the back door rather than the front door." Officials maintained that the canceled national scheme was fundamentally different from the services still being developed, and that people would retain alternatives to digital identification. National digital ID may be officially dead, but between One Login, digital wallets, and dozens of planned credentials, Whitehall still has plenty of identity-related work to keep it busy. ®

item.title: UK finance watchdog wants firms to report AI failures and close calls
item.description: The UK's financial regulator says firms' incident reporting must cover significant AI failures and near-misses as increasingly autonomous systems raise new risks. Speaking at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series on Monday, Financial Conduct Authority chief data, information and intelligence officer Jessica Rusu said the regulator wants Britain to lead safe AI adoption in financial services. Greater autonomy, however, requires clear accountability. "Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities, and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale," she said. "Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognized, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too." The UK punches above its weight in financial services. The sector contributed £223.6 billion to the UK economy in 2025 , or 8 percent of national output. That share was the fourth highest among OECD countries. Last week, UK artificial intelligence minister Kanishka Narayan said the government plans to work with Parliament and technical experts to assess how it could strengthen the regime to better protect Britain from AI-driven cyber threats and loss-of-control risks. "That includes identifying and reporting on serious incidents and near misses, including reducing AI-driven risk across essential services, and ensuring serious AI incidents can be properly reviewed," he said. Steven Adler, co-founder and chief scientist of independent nonprofit Guidelight AI Standards, also told MPs last week that AI oversight could learn from aviation, where reporting of near-misses is mandatory in most jurisdictions. "The way this works in aviation is that you not only want to learn about the serious crashes where someone has in fact died; you want to learn about the near-misses, because you can learn from those and help avoid them in the future," he said. However, the government has yet to commit to adding AI-specific measures to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill. Alexandra Jones, Director General for Growth, Science and International at the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, told MPs last week that amendments remain under consideration. In January, the House of Commons Treasury Committee called on financial regulators to conduct stress tests to ensure businesses are ready for AI-driven market shocks. The committee said there should be clear lines of accountability when AI systems produce harmful or unfair outcomes. ®

item.title: Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline
item.description: Services restored for most users, but power fault stalled hearings and left Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC customers unable to pay or move money An outage at Google’s cloud services in the UK has caused widespread disruption, hitting courts and leaving millions of customers unable to access or send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut. Google blamed a “power event” for the failure at its London-based Cloud computing operations on Tuesday, which affected its “europe-west2-b zone”. Continue reading...

item.title: Google Cloud's London zones takes a nap, multiple services disrupted
item.description: UPDATED Google Cloud customers in Western Europe are waking up to severe disruption affecting multiple services and, as yet, there is no estimated time of recovery. The europe-west-2-b is one of three local availability zones in the London region, intended to help protect against hardware or regional failures. The downtime began at 0608 UTC, meaning customers need more than a coffee to feel OK about today. According to Google Cloud’s status page : “Multiple Google Cloud services are experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region.” BigQuery Data TransferService, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Managed Service for Apache Kafka are all impacted, the tech biz confirmed. “Our engineering team continues to investigate the issue,” Google added. “We apologize to all who are affected by the disruption.” Techies on Reddit said the interruption was having a cascading affect on multiple suppliers. One said: “ oh man the classic one zone takes a nap and your non-HA service is in it.” “Loads of stuff seems to be down, DNS somewhere,” mused another. Over on the platform formerly known as Twitter, customers weren’t any happier - but that’s par for the course for people that use Elon Musk’s X. “Major GCP incident affecting Europe regions, good start to the day,” said one . According to Down Detector , multiple customers are caught up including Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Royal Mail, Rightmove, DPD, BT, Screwfix and Revolut. “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused,” said Revolut . Workarounds? “None for now now,” Google said. It plans to update customers at around 0930 UTC. ® Updated at 10.18 UTC on October 20, 2026, to add: Google has updated its status page to say Studio is not impacted by this outage and told customers looking for a workaround: "If feasible, the impacted customer may try to migrate their workload impacted to another available location."

item.title: London’s mobile networks fall to bottom of Europe’s capital league
item.description: London's mobile network performance has slipped behind other European capitals as operators struggle to add capacity fast enough to meet demand. The city ranked seventh out of 18 in the continent for median download speed in 2021, but traffic has since expanded faster than available capacity. Other metropolises have improved; London now has the slowest speeds and the highest latency under load, according to mobile network testing firm Ookla . The research points to obstacles mobile operators face in adding extra capacity: applications for new street masts in London have fallen since 2022, and about three quarters of those filed since 2019 were refused. The Big Smoke was among the first European capitals to get 5G coverage, yet when Ookla's Q3 2026 tests found the city now has the slowest median download speed (109.43 Mbps), the slowest median upload speed (11.40 Mbps) and the highest latency under load - a measure of how the network copes with heavy use. Ookla's records show London’s 5G medina speed peaked at 200 Mbps in Q2 2021, fell as low as 102 Mbps in Q3 2023, then recovered slightly. Paris, by contrast, has stayed above 225 Mbps since mid-2021. The cause is congestion. In Central London, performance slumps on weekdays as commuters arrive: median download speed falls to 80.07 Mbps through the morning, 27 percent below weekend levels at the same hours. Part of the problem is that UK mobile operators own few of their antenna sites, many of which sit on rooftops in built-up areas, says Ookla. Under the Electronic Communications Code, and changes introduced in 2017, a London rooftop is worth about £1,000 ($1,333) a year to its owner, down from £21,000 ($28k). That givers landlords little motivation to host antennas, and many prefer solar panels. Operators can also receive notices to quit when a building is redeveloped, and it is estimated that this keeps about 7 percent of London’s rooftop sites out of action at any time. Planning rules compound the problem as applications for new masts are more likely to be refused in boroughs with conservation areas, such as Westminster. Street mast applications peaked in 2020, early in the first 5G build, and have fallen by more than four-fifths since 2022. Three quarters of applications for new street masts since 2019 were refused, against one in five upgrades. "Planning restrictions, particularly in conservation areas, make it harder to install and upgrade the mobile equipment London needs," Ookla lead industry analyst Luke Kehoe told The Register . "Notices to quit can also force rooftop sites offline during redevelopment long before replacements are ready, leaving operators trying to restore lost capacity while demand keeps growing." City Hall has noticed, and a draft plan for the capital drawn up by the Mayor of London observes that notices to quit "have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities." item.dc:creator: Dan Robinson
item.content:encoded: London's mobile network performance has slipped behind other European capitals as operators struggle to add capacity fast enough to meet demand. The city ranked seventh out of 18 in the continent for median download speed in 2021, but traffic has since expanded faster than available capacity. Other metropolises have improved; London now has the slowest speeds and the highest latency under load, according to mobile network testing firm Ookla . The research points to obstacles mobile operators face in adding extra capacity: applications for new street masts in London have fallen since 2022, and about three quarters of those filed since 2019 were refused. The Big Smoke was among the first European capitals to get 5G coverage, yet when Ookla's Q3 2026 tests found the city now has the slowest median download speed (109.43 Mbps), the slowest median upload speed (11.40 Mbps) and the highest latency under load - a measure of how the network copes with heavy use. Ookla's records show London’s 5G medina speed peaked at 200 Mbps in Q2 2021, fell as low as 102 Mbps in Q3 2023, then recovered slightly. Paris, by contrast, has stayed above 225 Mbps since mid-2021. The cause is congestion. In Central London, performance slumps on weekdays as commuters arrive: median download speed falls to 80.07 Mbps through the morning, 27 percent below weekend levels at the same hours. Part of the problem is that UK mobile operators own few of their antenna sites, many of which sit on rooftops in built-up areas, says Ookla. Under the Electronic Communications Code, and changes introduced in 2017, a London rooftop is worth about £1,000 ($1,333) a year to its owner, down from £21,000 ($28k). That givers landlords little motivation to host antennas, and many prefer solar panels. Operators can also receive notices to quit when a building is redeveloped, and it is estimated that this keeps about 7 percent of London’s rooftop sites out of action at any time. Planning rules compound the problem as applications for new masts are more likely to be refused in boroughs with conservation areas, such as Westminster. Street mast applications peaked in 2020, early in the first 5G build, and have fallen by more than four-fifths since 2022. Three quarters of applications for new street masts since 2019 were refused, against one in five upgrades. "Planning restrictions, particularly in conservation areas, make it harder to install and upgrade the mobile equipment London needs," Ookla lead industry analyst Luke Kehoe told The Register . "Notices to quit can also force rooftop sites offline during redevelopment long before replacements are ready, leaving operators trying to restore lost capacity while demand keeps growing." City Hall has noticed, and a draft plan for the capital drawn up by the Mayor of London observes that notices to quit "have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities." The plan, due tor adoption in 2028, would require developers to keep mobile service running during construction, put masts on taller buildings and in the public realm; and ask boroughs to work with operators on sites in conservation areas. Other experts blame different factors for London’s poor mobile service. Professor Mohamed-Slim Alouini of the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) told The Register last year that the government’s decision to rip-and-replace network equipment supplied by China-based vendor Huawei had diverted funds that should have gone into building more capacity. He also said 5G was overhyped early on, leading to a perception among users that it wasn’t really worth having and operators reluctant to invest. Whatever the cause, London’s mobile experience now trails its European peers, though people elsewhere in the UK who still can’t get a 5G signal will have little sympathy. ®

item.title: Why cyber resilience is now a boardroom priority for UK public services
item.description: The UK public sector has reached a cyber resilience inflection point. A new Prime Minister has taken office, and significant machinery-of-government changes have already been announced, including the scrapping of DSIT, the department that had become the center of government digital, technology and cyber policy. Its responsibilities are now being redistributed across other parts of Whitehall, creating a new policy and delivery landscape for public sector leaders to navigate. For years, cyber security was treated as a specialist operational discipline that was essential but largely delegated to technical teams. That model is no longer sustainable. Pressure is now coming from three directions at once, as policy raises expectations for boards and senior leaders, organizational reform reshapes how services, systems and suppliers connect, and technology change, from cloud and hybrid work to AI, expands both opportunity and exposure. Together, these forces mean cyber resilience can no longer sit below board level. Public services, from healthcare and benefits to transport, education, local government and emergency response, are now so digitally dependent that a cyber incident is not simply an IT outage. It is a risk to public trust, public safety and the continuity of government itself. Recent history shows what this means in practice. The 2024 ransomware attack on Synnovis, a pathology services provider to parts of the NHS, significantly reduced the capacity to process blood, urine and specimen tests, caused disruption across south-east London and contributed to delays affecting more than 11,000 outpatient and elective procedure appointments. Incidents like this turn abstract cyber risk into real-world service disruption, making resilience a boardroom issue rather than a back-office concern. Cyber resilience is no longer a technical aspiration, but a leadership obligation shaped by policy, organizational and technology change. Policy change has made cyber resilience a leadership obligation The direction from government and the National Cyber Security Centre is clear. The Cyber Resilience Pledge asks organizations to make cyber security a board-level responsibility, register for NCSC Early Warning and take a risk-based approach to Cyber Essentials across their supply chains. The NCSC’s Cyber Governance Code of Practice reinforces the point that cyber risk must be governed like any other material organizational risk. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will further expand expectations across essential and digital services, strengthening incident reporting and bringing more critical suppliers into scope. This matters because the scale and impact of cyber threats facing the UK are increasing sharply. The NCSC handled 204 nationally significant cyber incidents in the year to September 2025, up from 89 the previous year. item.dc:creator: Richard Spalding
item.content:encoded: The UK public sector has reached a cyber resilience inflection point. A new Prime Minister has taken office, and significant machinery-of-government changes have already been announced, including the scrapping of DSIT, the department that had become the center of government digital, technology and cyber policy. Its responsibilities are now being redistributed across other parts of Whitehall, creating a new policy and delivery landscape for public sector leaders to navigate. For years, cyber security was treated as a specialist operational discipline that was essential but largely delegated to technical teams. That model is no longer sustainable. Pressure is now coming from three directions at once, as policy raises expectations for boards and senior leaders, organizational reform reshapes how services, systems and suppliers connect, and technology change, from cloud and hybrid work to AI, expands both opportunity and exposure. Together, these forces mean cyber resilience can no longer sit below board level. Public services, from healthcare and benefits to transport, education, local government and emergency response, are now so digitally dependent that a cyber incident is not simply an IT outage. It is a risk to public trust, public safety and the continuity of government itself. Recent history shows what this means in practice. The 2024 ransomware attack on Synnovis, a pathology services provider to parts of the NHS, significantly reduced the capacity to process blood, urine and specimen tests, caused disruption across south-east London and contributed to delays affecting more than 11,000 outpatient and elective procedure appointments. Incidents like this turn abstract cyber risk into real-world service disruption, making resilience a boardroom issue rather than a back-office concern. Cyber resilience is no longer a technical aspiration, but a leadership obligation shaped by policy, organizational and technology change. Policy change has made cyber resilience a leadership obligation The direction from government and the National Cyber Security Centre is clear. The Cyber Resilience Pledge asks organizations to make cyber security a board-level responsibility, register for NCSC Early Warning and take a risk-based approach to Cyber Essentials across their supply chains. The NCSC’s Cyber Governance Code of Practice reinforces the point that cyber risk must be governed like any other material organizational risk. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will further expand expectations across essential and digital services, strengthening incident reporting and bringing more critical suppliers into scope. This matters because the scale and impact of cyber threats facing the UK are increasing sharply. The NCSC handled 204 nationally significant cyber incidents in the year to September 2025, up from 89 the previous year. That means the UK is now experiencing an average of four nationally significant cyber attacks every week. Policy has therefore changed the boardroom question. Leaders should no longer ask only whether an organization has invested in security tools. They need to ask whether they can prove resilience, evidence accountability and continue delivering critical services when systems are under pressure, suppliers are compromised, data access is disrupted or attackers are already inside the network. Organisational change is creating hidden cyber risk The second force is organizational change. Local Government Reorganisation is redrawing structures and responsibilities across England. Rail renationalization and other shifts in public ownership are changing who owns, manages and secures critical data and systems. Departmental priorities and delivery models are also evolving under a new Prime Minister, with DSIT being dismantled and functions including digital transformation, public sector AI adoption, information resilience and online harms moving into different departments and central government structures. Every one of these transitions creates potential gaps. Systems need to be integrated. Identity and access privileges need to be reassessed. Data needs to move between teams, agencies and suppliers. Contracts and responsibilities need to be redefined. During periods of change, the attack surface expands, and accountability can become blurred. This is why cyber resilience must be built into public sector reform from the outset. The question is not simply how to restructure services efficiently. It is how to ensure citizens can continue to access those services securely throughout the transition. Reorganization without resilience is a risk to the public. Technology change demands continuous assurance The third force is technology change. Public sector work now happens across hybrid environments, shared services, cloud platforms, partner ecosystems and complex supply chains. Traditional security models were built for a more stable world of fixed offices, predictable networks, known users and clearly defined organizational boundaries. That world no longer exists. AI makes this problem more urgent. AI is already being used across the public sector to improve productivity, analyze information and support better service delivery. But without governance, organizations can quickly lose track of which tools are being used, what data they can access and whether sensitive information is being exposed. Shadow AI is not a future risk. It is a present governance challenge. Resilience in this environment requires continuous assurance. Access should not be granted simply because a user is on a trusted network. Every request should be verified based on identity, context, device posture and risk. Users should only receive the access they need, when they need it. Applications should be protected from unnecessary exposure. Data should be segmented so that compromise in one area does not automatically spread across the organization. What public sector boards should do now Making cyber resilience a board-level priority does not mean every director needs to become a technical expert. It means senior leaders need the right governance, evidence and accountability to respond to the three forces reshaping risk across the public sector. That starts with treating cyber resilience as a standing board agenda item, linked directly to service continuity, citizen trust, regulatory exposure and reform delivery. It also requires boards to understand which critical services depend on which systems, suppliers and datasets, where single points of failure exist, and how disruption in one part of the ecosystem could affect citizens’ ability to access essential services. Supply chain assurance must be part of that same conversation. Public services are delivered through ecosystems, so resilience cannot stop at the boundary of a single department, council, agency or trust. Cyber Essentials, supplier checks, contractual obligations and clear incident reporting expectations should be embedded into procurement and contract management. At the same time, public bodies need to move away from implicit trust based on networks or locations and towards continuous verification based on identity, context, device posture and risk. Users should have only the access they need, when they need it, and AI adoption should be governed before it scales so innovation does not create unmanaged routes to sensitive information. Resilience is now a test of public sector leadership The UK’s policy environment has changed. Public sector organizations are changing. Technology is changing even faster. The only way to manage that complexity is to build cyber resilience into the way public services are governed, transformed and delivered. The public sector cannot afford to treat resilience as something to retrofit after legislation tightens, reform programs are complete or AI adoption has already accelerated. It must be designed in from the outset, measured at leadership level and tested continuously. Cyb

item.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
item.description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. Continue reading...

item.title: Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?
item.description: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner ‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant. Not just yet, judging by the extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year : it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger. Continue reading...

item.title: Japan launches mission to bring home a piece of the Martian moon Phobos
item.description: Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, a daring international project that could yield new insights into the formation of the Solar System. The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan. The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan's flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan's heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. Read full article Comments

item.title: Sony updates the Walkman as a $5,900 gold-plated MP3 player
item.description: Sony last week revived its famed Walkman brand of portable music players, with a trio of updated products that feature Android 16, touch screens, eye-popping prices, and dubious assertions of audiophile appeal. The Japanese giant named the new models the NW-WM1ZM3, NW-WM1AM3 and NW-ZX900. All can store and play many codecs, including MP3s, WMA, and FLAC files, plus others like Direct Stream Digital (DSD) and Apple Lossless, which use various tricks to avoid nasty artefacts accruing during the digitization process. Sony also says it has used “key components made from oxygen-free copper” because that apparently delivers “uncompromising sound quality.” The machines also include “screws featuring a low-resistance gold-plated treatment … providing a stable ground connection that delivers powerful bass, an expansive soundstage and smooth, extended high frequencies.” Sony claims even the cabling it’s used in the devices “further reduces noise and preserves signal integrity for rich, detailed sound.” They’re also housed in carefully-milled slabs of copper – gold-plated in the case of the NW-WM1ZM3 – because that apparently improves sound, too. And then Sony’s gone and spoiled it all by offering Bluetooth connectivity, a notorious music-mangler, in addition to wired headphone ports. Sony’s US site lists all three devices, which run Android 16 and include Wi-Fi so they can access streaming music services. All are USB-chargeable and Sony claims their batteries allow 30-odd hours of music playback. The NW-ZX900 packs a five-inch touch screen and 64GB of onboard memory. It’s the baby of the range at just $1,900. The NW-WM1AM3 will set you back $3,000, which buys 128GB of memory and a 5.5-inch screen. The flagship NW-WM1ZM3 has the same size screen and includes 256GB of memory. It’s also a ‘Droid. Don’t bother trying to put these under a Christmas tree because Sony says it will ship them mid-January. ®

item.content:encoded: Sony last week revived its famed Walkman brand of portable music players, with a trio of updated products that feature Android 16, touch screens, eye-popping prices, and dubious assertions of audiophile appeal. The Japanese giant named the new models the NW-WM1ZM3, NW-WM1AM3 and NW-ZX900. All can store and play many codecs, including MP3s, WMA, and FLAC files, plus others like Direct Stream Digital (DSD) and Apple Lossless, which use various tricks to avoid nasty artefacts accruing during the digitization process. Sony also says it has used “key components made from oxygen-free copper” because that apparently delivers “uncompromising sound quality.” The machines also include “screws featuring a low-resistance gold-plated treatment … providing a stable ground connection that delivers powerful bass, an expansive soundstage and smooth, extended high frequencies.” Sony claims even the cabling it’s used in the devices “further reduces noise and preserves signal integrity for rich, detailed sound.” They’re also housed in carefully-milled slabs of copper – gold-plated in the case of the NW-WM1ZM3 – because that apparently improves sound, too. And then Sony’s gone and spoiled it all by offering Bluetooth connectivity, a notorious music-mangler, in addition to wired headphone ports. Sony’s US site lists all three devices, which run Android 16 and include Wi-Fi so they can access streaming music services. All are USB-chargeable and Sony claims their batteries allow 30-odd hours of music playback. The NW-ZX900 packs a five-inch touch screen and 64GB of onboard memory. It’s the baby of the range at just $1,900. The NW-WM1AM3 will set you back $3,000, which buys 128GB of memory and a 5.5-inch screen. The flagship NW-WM1ZM3 has the same size screen and includes 256GB of memory. It’s also a ‘Droid. Don’t bother trying to put these under a Christmas tree because Sony says it will ship them mid-January. ®

item.title: ‘David Beckham’ was briefly the world’s second-worst manga pirate
item.description: A website registered by “David Beckham” was the world’s second-most-visited source of pirated Japanese manga in February 2025, leading publishers to call for better verification of who buys domain names to address the problem. The “Beckham” who registered the site was of course not the famous footballer and spokesmodel. However Tatsuo Ninoseki, an attorney with the Shin Hirakawa-Cho Law Office who represents the Japan Publishers manga Anti-Piracy Conference (JPMAC), put fake Becks in play today during a session on DNS abuse at ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali, Indonesia. Ninoseki said miscreants routinely create unauthorized English translations of manga and post them on websites that include ads. The lawyer said such sites can attract hundreds of millions of users and cost publishers $17 billion in revenue each year. JPMAC has decided its best course of action is not to pursue copyright abusers, but instead to go after commercial-scale pirates. That means it tries to act against pirate websites like those registered by “Beckham,” by sending them stern legal letters and using other legal means. But those pirates have trained to get around defenders. Ninoseki said pirate manga sites maintain a set of domain names – he said they’ve registered names in 158 top-level domains and frequently “domain hop” between them. The pirates’ pools of domains include some common naming elements, so even though Google has stopped indexing these pirate sites, users figure out that a theoretical piratemanga.XXX site will soon reappear at piratemanga.YYY. Pirate sites also redirect from domains they’re not using to host content to another that is full of pirated comics. Sometimes they use several sites at once and direct users across a fleet of live sites, so traffic flows to each site stay small and don’t cause suspicion. Ninoseki said 82.4 percent of domain hops happen within 15 days of the last move, suggesting pirates know how long enforcement actions or takedown requests will take and move to a different site before they run into trouble. “Many domain hops do not appear to be a reaction to legal countermeasures,” the attorney said. Ninoseki said JPMAC feels more comprehensive verification of domain name registrants would be a big help, especially checking physical addresses provided by registrants which he feels would weed out more pirates. The lawyer spoke during an ICANN session on DNS abuse, which the governance body defines as using domain names to facilitate malware, botnets, phishing, pharming, and spam. ICANN is currently working on a policy called PDP1 to address DNS abuse, one element of which would require registries to consider all domains held by their customers if just one is found to conduct DNS abuse. That policy would mean that once a registrant named “David Beckham” is connected to a single piracy site, all other domains registered by fake Becks would be checked in case they’re also committing DNS fouls. ®

To find out why, and how, Ian Sample speaks to Dr Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security and the Bloomberg School of Public Health. item.title: ICANN testing tech to let law enforcement access non-public WHOIS info
item.description: ICANN has started testing authentication schemes that will allow law enforcement agencies to make urgent requests for non-public WHOIS information – when needed to address threats to life, critical infrastructure, or child exploitation. Domain registrars collect information about their customers and in the past that data was publicly available in WHOIS records. Some domain registrars offer services that substitute their own contact details, to preserve customer privacy. In recent years, laws like GDPR mean registrars are sometimes required to hide WHOIS data. That’s fair enough but makes it hard for law enforcement to contact a domain holder if their resources are being misused – intentionally or otherwise – for purposes such as hosting malware, acting as command-and-control infrastructure for malware, or facilitating phishing. ICANN’s definition for the kind of behaviour it thinks justifies urgent requests for WHOIS info is “imminent threat to life, of serious bodily injury, to critical infrastructure, or of child exploitation.” The org has convened an Input Group on Law Enforcement Agency Authentication Mechanisms to consider the issue, and that group yesterday explained its progress during ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali, Indonesia. At this point, readers may have concerns that this proposal could allow law enforcement authorities to make inappropriate requests for WHOIS information. Several factors may ease such concerns. One is that representatives of domain registrars Namecheap and Verisign spoke during the session about the proposal, and both were supportive. Another is that the Input Group’s work is largely technical. Once it devises a mechanism to allow requests, other groups within ICANN dedicated to policy will work out acceptable use and related issues. This is the way internet governance gets done! Specialists work on their own bits of a problem and then collaborate to create a robust system that works at a technical level, is practical, and enforceable in multiple jurisdictions. How they’ll do it At this point, ICANN’s preferred approach is to use Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) so that authenticated users at law enforcement agencies can log into the governance org’s Registration Data Request Service (RDRS) and file requests to access non-public WHOIS info. ICANN is already testing this approach with the FBI and Interpol but is open to other authentication mechanisms to allow other agencies access RDRS. The Input Group’s aim is to publish a spec those agencies can conform to. ICANN will pass requests filed in RDRS to whichever registrar sold the domain. The registrar will have 24 hours to consider the request – or up to 72 hours for complex queries. Registrars will also be able to deny requests if they feel the query does not meet the urgency threshold. Register readers might worry that a colossal agency like the FBI could flood RDRS with requests from thousands of individual agents, swamping domain registries. ICANN’s plan

Register readers might worry that a colossal agency like the FBI could flood RDRS with requests from thousands of individual agents, swamping domain registries. ICANN’s plan is to avoid that by requiring law enforcement agencies to nominate certain personnel who are permitted to make requests, and to enforce that permission using a token shared during SAML handshakes. The content of that token is the kind of policy question that the Input Group expects others at ICANN to finalize later. Another issue under consideration is how to protect the identity of law enforcement workers who make RDRS requests, as ICANN feels they could become targets of harassment (or worse) if their requests to see WHOIS data include email addresses. ®

item.title: DeepSeek deep-sixed at all US federal civilian agencies
item.description: The US Department of Homeland Security on Monday issued an order directing federal civilian agencies not to use technology products from Chinese AI lab DeepSeek, and to remove any existing implementations. The order [PDF] is broad, as it requires agencies to ditch "all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations." Complying will be tricky as it is not clear which third-party products and services have been developed using DeepSeek's wares. Nor is it clear whether "developed using" means providing ongoing access to DeepSeek models via API or simply refers to any app vibe-coded with the help of DeepSeek. It also leaves open the question of AI gateways. Services such as OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway make DeepSeek's models available through APIs. And those using gateway services may find themselves using DeepSeek models without meaning to do so. OpenRouter, for example , "routes requests to the best available providers for your model." It selects what the service deems to be the best fit provider of AI services. Vercel AI Gateway does the same by default . So federal civilian agencies could be using DeepSeek models inadvertently, if they haven't taken steps to constrain their AI providers. A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. US officials have contemplated a ban on DeepSeek since the China-based AI lab released DeepSeek-R1 in early 2025. On February 6, 2025, US Representative Darin LaHood (R-IL) and US Representative Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) introduced the No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act. The lawmakers characterised DeepSeek as a national security threat because its AI models purportedly capture data on US citizens and provide it to the Chinese government. The bill never made it out of committee, but various government agencies followed through. The US Defense community and lawmakers have already exiled DeepSeek. The Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) started blocking DeepSeek on the Pentagon’s IT networks in January 2025. The US Navy , NASA , and the US House of Representatives took similar steps. So did various US states. While the DHS announcement has taken a long time to reach civilian agencies, its timing may be a boon for American AI companies which, like Anthropic, hope to soon go public. That's because open weight models represent competition, and those from China have proven particularly popular both in terms of capabilities and cost. Government agencies that cannot deploy such models (and the taxpayers who fund those agencies) may be stuck paying the prices set by favored US model makers. Concerns about the security and privacy of DeepSeek's iOS mobile app surfaced shortly after DeepSeek-R1 debuted . item.dc:creator: Thomas Claburn
item.content:encoded: The US Department of Homeland Security on Monday issued an order directing federal civilian agencies not to use technology products from Chinese AI lab DeepSeek, and to remove any existing implementations. The order [PDF] is broad, as it requires agencies to ditch "all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations." Complying will be tricky as it is not clear which third-party products and services have been developed using DeepSeek's wares. Nor is it clear whether "developed using" means providing ongoing access to DeepSeek models via API or simply refers to any app vibe-coded with the help of DeepSeek. It also leaves open the question of AI gateways. Services such as OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway make DeepSeek's models available through APIs. And those using gateway services may find themselves using DeepSeek models without meaning to do so. OpenRouter, for example , "routes requests to the best available providers for your model." It selects what the service deems to be the best fit provider of AI services. Vercel AI Gateway does the same by default . So federal civilian agencies could be using DeepSeek models inadvertently, if they haven't taken steps to constrain their AI providers. A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. US officials have contemplated a ban on DeepSeek since the China-based AI lab released DeepSeek-R1 in early 2025. On February 6, 2025, US Representative Darin LaHood (R-IL) and US Representative Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) introduced the No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act. The lawmakers characterised DeepSeek as a national security threat because its AI models purportedly capture data on US citizens and provide it to the Chinese government. The bill never made it out of committee, but various government agencies followed through. The US Defense community and lawmakers have already exiled DeepSeek. The Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) started blocking DeepSeek on the Pentagon’s IT networks in January 2025. The US Navy , NASA , and the US House of Representatives took similar steps. So did various US states. While the DHS announcement has taken a long time to reach civilian agencies, its timing may be a boon for American AI companies which, like Anthropic, hope to soon go public. That's because open weight models represent competition, and those from China have proven particularly popular both in terms of capabilities and cost. Government agencies that cannot deploy such models (and the taxpayers who fund those agencies) may be stuck paying the prices set by favored US model makers. Concerns about the security and privacy of DeepSeek's iOS mobile app surfaced shortly after DeepSeek-R1 debuted . Several months later, a December 2025 report on the DeekSeek mobile app for Android and iOS cited similar concerns, including plaintext information leaks, links to servers run by Chinese tech firms, and shortcomings like lack of SSL pinning. These issues, however, are mainly mobile security problems that afflict many apps, particularly those that integrate third-party advertising SDKs from companies based outside the US. They don't really address the additional risks posed by the capture of text prompts and responses, or how local secrets and other sensitive information can be ingested by AI agents. Katie Moussouris, founder and CEO of Luta Security , told The Register in an email that while there are legitimate national security reasons to keep DeepSeek's app and servers away from government systems, the way this particular order is written exceeds that requirement in ways that aren't practical. "Banning DeepSeek's own app and API is workable," said Moussouris. "The problem is the ban on 'third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations.' The order doesn't say what 'developed using' means. It could technically cover any model derived from DeepSeek and more importantly, any software whose developers used DeepSeek to write or test code. An AI software bill of materials doesn't record which tools developers used, so it would be no real help. Every vendor would have to attest that nothing it relies on ever touched DeepSeek. There's no practical way to verify that." Moussouris also took issue with the breadth of the order, noting that applying the rules to US-hosted versions of DeepSeek's models goes too far. "The risks the order cites are mostly about data flowing to DeepSeek's servers in China, its data collection, and its app," she said. "US hosting avoids most of those. "For the model itself, the order says only that it may contain malware or vulnerabilities, which is true of all software. NIST found DeepSeek more vulnerable to prompt injection than US models , though every model has that problem. NIST also found it easier to jailbreak , but jailbreak guardrails often get in the way of defenders." ®

item.title: Pennsylvania issues alert on congenital measles—something US hasn't seen for decades
item.description: Pennsylvania's health department issued a health alert Monday as cases of measles in pregnancy and, in turn, cases of congenital measles have continued to increase. Before the current outbreak—which continues to rage across the state—congenital measles cases hadn't been seen in decades, the department noted in its advisory. The alert included detailed clinical guidance for managing measles exposures and cases during pregnancy as well as cases in newborns. Many doctors have never seen such cases in their careers given the decades of successful use of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But now, with vaccination rates slipping nationwide, the highly infectious virus is better able to get footholds in communities and spread rapidly through under-vaccinated pockets, as is happening in Pennsylvania. As of October 19, Pennsylvania had reported 1,286 measles cases this year across 42 counties. Of those, 247 have been hospitalized, and six people have reportedly died (though the latest reported death is still pending an investigation by the state health department before it is added to the state tally). Read full article Comments

item.title: Russian spacecraft maneuvers in "extreme proximity" to satellite used by Ukraine
item.description: A Russian military satellite maneuvered in "extreme proximity" of a commercial Earth-imaging satellite in recent days in the first known example an unsanctioned rendezvous in low-Earth orbit, according to orbital intelligence company LeoLabs. The Russian spacecraft, Kosmos 2612, "conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers toward ICEYE-X36, a US-operated commercial imaging satellite," LeoLabs said. "Kosmos 2612 closed from hundreds of kilometers away to extreme proximity to ICEYE-X36. It then maneuvered around ICEYE-X36, remained nearby for an extended period, and then began moving away." US military officials and independent analysts have tracked Kosmos 2612 since its April launch on a Soyuz rocket from a spaceport in northern Russia. Within weeks, it became apparent that at least four of the six satellites from that launch were stalking ICEYE-X36 after they adjusted orbits to line up with the orbit of the ICEYE spacecraft. Read full article Comments

Within weeks, it became apparent that at least four of the six satellites from that launch were stalking ICEYE-X36 after they adjusted orbits to line up with the orbit of the ICEYE spacecraft. item.title: Grocery giant Ahold Delhaize confirms cyberattack forced US and European systems offline
item.description: Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack, affecting most of its US and European brands. The multinational chain originally disclosed the incident on October 12. “Ahold Delhaize is experiencing a security issue within its network,” it said at the time, adding that security teams, working to mitigate the issues, took “some” IT systems offline. On Monday, the company confirmed that it proactively took certain IT systems, including websites and apps, offline, affecting most of its brands, and said that “malicious actions of others” caused the security issue. “Taking systems offline to help protect them was a precautionary measure that affected most of our brands across Europe and the United States,” Frans Muller, president and CEO of Ahold Delhaize, said in a Monday statement. “The investigation to date confirms this was the right decision.” At this time, all of the physical stores remain open, and the investigation hasn’t uncovered any evidence to suggest the miscreants stole any “sensitive customer, associate, or partner data,” the disclosure said. The company last week notified the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre about the digital intruders, and on Monday filed a report with the Dutch police, according to the statement. Albert Heijn’s website and app are back online, and the company expects home deliveries to resume on Friday. Belgian e-commerce is fully operational, and e-commerce services at Ahold Delhaize’s American brands (Food Lion, Giant Food, Martin’s, Hannaford, and Stop & Shop) are expected to work “in the coming days.” The Etos and Gall & Gall websites are also up and running, along with the “majority of websites and apps” across brands serving central and southeastern Europe. Ahold Delhaize did not immediately respond to The Register ’s questions about the cyberattack, including whether it was linked to attacks on refrigeration controllers at hundreds of French supermarkets beginning October 11. The attacks reportedly pushed temperatures as high as 122°F (50°C), spoiling food and causing fires at some locations. This latest cyberattack is Ahold Delhaize’s second in two years. A November 2024 digital break-in disrupted brands across the organization, with some Stop & Shop stores struggling to fill prescriptions, while Food Lion employees reported delayed and missing deliveries. INC Ransom claimed responsibility for the attack at the time and leaked some documents reportedly taken from the retailer's systems. Ahold Delhaize ultimately determined more than 2.2 million people’s data - including personal, financial, and health details - had been compromised. ®

item.title: Amazon makes vague commitment to unproven nuclear tech to power Indiana datacenters
item.description: To feed its Indiana datacenters with plenty of juice, Amazon is funding the development of a new nuclear facility that will provide nearly 1 gigawatt of power. However, we'll have to see if this happens anytime soon, given the immature technology it's using. Amazon said on Monday that it was funding the project with an undisclosed amount of cash as part of an expansion of its existing deal with X-energy , a next-generation nuclear power startup focusing on building small modular reactors (SMRs) powered by Tri-Structural ISOtropic (TRISO) fuel pellets and cooled by helium gas. Amazon would tell us only that it’s “investing billions in nuclear energy projects” without getting specific on this project. According to X-energy, the project will see Amazon fund the development of 12 of those SMRs, its Xe-100 model, in Sullivan County, Indiana, at the site of a former coal power plant. Once up and running, the facility will supply 960 megawatts of grid-connected electricity, with Amazon contracting as the first power purchaser from the future plant. As for when it might come online, that’s anyone’s guess. Amazon wouldn’t tell us, only pointing us to an article in Indiana newspaper the South Bend Tribune in which an X-energy representative said it could be completed “as early as the mid-2030s,” though “the timeline could change the further the project gets developed.” That’s quite likely given X-energy’s current status and the state of next-generation nuclear power more generally, and to understand why it helps to understand how nuclear permitting works in the US. First off, despite the promises , hype , and mountains of cash poured into nuclear power by the tech industry, the US has yet to build a single operable SMR. China and Russia have built functional SMRs. A single experimental unit has achieved criticality in the US, but it’s not a functional, power-producing reactor and was only built to demonstrate the ability for a specific design to become one. The company with that experimental US SMR is not X-energy, who has yet to build a working reactor. As to how reactors get approved in the US, there are two pathways that nuclear power companies can pursue: One is to get a standard design approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). That pathway gives a company license to build a reactor of a specific model wherever they want, as the design has been deemed safe independent of any physical site. That means the certified reactor can be sold and built without the need for the NRC to recertify the core design each time a project gets underway. There is only one company in the US that has a standard design approval for an SMR: Nuscale , which has yet to build a single reactor, has no projects under construction, and has already abandoned a Utah plant due to lack of interest from power distributors. The other option allows SMR developers to get approval for a site-specific project, which is quicker and involves the NRC blessing a particular reactor i

item.content:encoded: To feed its Indiana datacenters with plenty of juice, Amazon is funding the development of a new nuclear facility that will provide nearly 1 gigawatt of power. However, we'll have to see if this happens anytime soon, given the immature technology it's using. Amazon said on Monday that it was funding the project with an undisclosed amount of cash as part of an expansion of its existing deal with X-energy , a next-generation nuclear power startup focusing on building small modular reactors (SMRs) powered by Tri-Structural ISOtropic (TRISO) fuel pellets and cooled by helium gas. Amazon would tell us only that it’s “investing billions in nuclear energy projects” without getting specific on this project. According to X-energy, the project will see Amazon fund the development of 12 of those SMRs, its Xe-100 model, in Sullivan County, Indiana, at the site of a former coal power plant. Once up and running, the facility will supply 960 megawatts of grid-connected electricity, with Amazon contracting as the first power purchaser from the future plant. As for when it might come online, that’s anyone’s guess. Amazon wouldn’t tell us, only pointing us to an article in Indiana newspaper the South Bend Tribune in which an X-energy representative said it could be completed “as early as the mid-2030s,” though “the timeline could change the further the project gets developed.” That’s quite likely given X-energy’s current status and the state of next-generation nuclear power more generally, and to understand why it helps to understand how nuclear permitting works in the US. First off, despite the promises , hype , and mountains of cash poured into nuclear power by the tech industry, the US has yet to build a single operable SMR. China and Russia have built functional SMRs. A single experimental unit has achieved criticality in the US, but it’s not a functional, power-producing reactor and was only built to demonstrate the ability for a specific design to become one. The company with that experimental US SMR is not X-energy, who has yet to build a working reactor. As to how reactors get approved in the US, there are two pathways that nuclear power companies can pursue: One is to get a standard design approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). That pathway gives a company license to build a reactor of a specific model wherever they want, as the design has been deemed safe independent of any physical site. That means the certified reactor can be sold and built without the need for the NRC to recertify the core design each time a project gets underway. There is only one company in the US that has a standard design approval for an SMR: Nuscale , which has yet to build a single reactor, has no projects under construction, and has already abandoned a Utah plant due to lack of interest from power distributors. The other option allows SMR developers to get approval for a site-specific project, which is quicker and involves the NRC blessing a particular reactor in a particular place. There have been several of those permits awarded, with Kairos Power being approved to build an SMR in Oak Ridge, Tennessee in partnership with Google, General Electric planning another SMR in Oak Ridge, and TerraPower inching forward with its own project in Wyoming despite delays . Notice X-energy isn’t mentioned there, either. The company claims that it’s in “the final phases” of NRC approval for a construction permit in Texas , where it’ll supply power for a Dow Chemical manufacturing plant, but that likely won’t matter too much for the Indiana project’s timeline. As mentioned above, nuclear construction permits are site specific, and the Texas plant only involves four reactors - far fewer than the 12 planned in Indiana. X-energy didn’t respond to questions for this story, but Amazon told us it's not going to be involved in any way with getting approval across the finish line for the Indiana plant. “Amazon's role is as an investor … as well as committing to being the first customer for power produced from the facility,” a company spokesperson told us. “New technologies like this often need initial customers to help de-risk projects and provide funding so they can be built and scaled to commercial availability, and that is the role Amazon is playing by helping to fund the project's development.” Like other large, ambitious next-generation nuclear projects, in other words, this one is just as much in the maybe column as the rest. ®

item.title: Accused OpenAI spy had folder called “Saudi Gov Docs,” FBI says
item.description: On Monday, a court granted the US government's request to deny release of a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a top-secret conference room to steal the frontier lab’s secrets. In a court filing Sunday, US attorney Craig Missakian argued that Abdulrahman Alfozan must continue to be detained while the US makes its case that Alfozan brazenly spied on OpenAI, either for his own personal business gain or to benefit the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Evidence showed that Alfozan had been chatting with a member of the KSA royal family on WhatsApp, while pursuing opportunities to permanently move back to Saudi Arabia during the country's biggest AI push yet, the government argued. Shortly before his arrest, the FBI found he accessed a folder called "Saudi Gov Docs" on his iPhone, where he also allegedly stored photos of a second bug he planted in the offices. Read full article Comments
